```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern typed-emitter
 * @options f4f2afcf27974e2a
 */

/**
 * Every event, and what it carries.
 *
 * The one declaration everything else is derived from. Adding an event here is
 * enough to make it emittable and subscribable; nothing needs to be registered
 * anywhere, and no string is written twice.
 *
 * Payloads are tuples rather than single objects, because a tuple is the
 * general case — a single payload is a tuple of one — and because naming the
 * elements puts those names in front of a caller writing the handler. A tuple
 * may be empty, and an event declared that way emits with no arguments at all.
 */
export interface OrderEvents {
  readonly opened: [];
  readonly paid: [id: string, amount: number];
  readonly cancelled: [id: string, reason: string];
}

/**
 * The names, derived rather than repeated.
 */
export type OrderEventName = keyof OrderEvents;

/**
 * What a subscriber looks like.
 *
 * The return type is `void`, which accepts a function returning anything —
 * including a promise. That is worth being explicit about, because it is the
 * one hole in synchronous dispatch: an `async` handler will run, `emit` will
 * not wait for it, and a rejection inside it will go unobserved. Asynchronous
 * dispatch exists for that case.
 *
 * A handler may declare fewer parameters than the event carries, which is
 * ordinary function assignability rather than an oversight — a subscriber that
 * only needs the first field should not have to name the rest.
 */
export type EventHandler<Payload extends readonly unknown[]> = (
  ...payload: Payload
) => void;

/**
 * Where the subscriptions live.
 *
 * The load-bearing choice in this file, and the reason nothing here contains a
 * cast. A `Map` keyed by the union of event names would lose the correspondence
 * between a key and its payload, so the handlers found under one name would
 * have the handler type of *every* name and dispatch would need an `as never`
 * to call one — which is how most implementations of this are written. A mapped
 * type keeps the pairing, so an index at `K extends keyof E` yields exactly
 * that event's handler type and the call typechecks on its own.
 *
 * Being generic in the event map is part of what makes that work, and it is not
 * obvious: specialise this to one map and *reading* still checks, while
 * *writing* stops, because at a generic key the compiler has to satisfy every
 * member the key could name at once. That is the version most emitters cast
 * their way out of. Keeping the map a parameter and fixing it in a subclass
 * below costs one declaration and removes the need.
 *
 * The value is a `Map` from handler to whether it was registered for a single
 * delivery. That is what makes `once` a property of the registration rather
 * than a wrapper around the function: a wrapper would have an identity the
 * caller never saw, and `off` with the original function would find nothing and
 * silently succeed. Insertion order is preserved, so registration order is
 * dispatch order.
 */
type Registry<E extends Record<keyof E, readonly unknown[]>> = {
  [K in keyof E]?: Map<EventHandler<E[K]>, boolean>;
};

/**
 * Where isolated failures go.
 *
 * Required rather than optional, and that is deliberate: isolation means a
 * subscriber can fail without the emitter or the other subscribers noticing,
 * which is only safe if the failure is reported somewhere. A default would make
 * the silence the easy path.
 */
export interface EmitterOptions<E extends Record<keyof E, readonly unknown[]>> {
  readonly onError: (error: unknown, event: keyof E) => void;
}

/**
 * The emitter.
 *
 * Generic in its event map rather than tied to one, which is what keeps the
 * registry free of casts, and reusable as a side effect: a second set of events
 * needs another subclass and nothing else.
 *
 * The surface is deliberately small: subscribe, subscribe once, unsubscribe,
 * emit, and count. Anything else an emitter is sometimes given — wildcards,
 * event inheritance, removing every listener at once — either cannot be typed
 * without giving up what the event map buys, or is a convenience that hides
 * which subscriptions were dropped.
 */
export class TypedEmitter<E extends Record<keyof E, readonly unknown[]>> {
  private readonly registry: Registry<E> = {};
  private readonly onError: (error: unknown, event: keyof E) => void;

  constructor(options: EmitterOptions<E>) {
    this.onError = options.onError;
  }

  /**
   * Subscribes, and returns the way to stop.
   *
   * The returned function is the reliable way to unsubscribe, because it closes
   * over both the event and the handler and so cannot be called with the wrong
   * pair. `off` exists for the case where the subscription and the teardown are
   * too far apart to share a closure.
   */
  on<K extends keyof E>(event: K, handler: EventHandler<E[K]>): () => void {
    return this.add(event, handler, false);
  }

  /**
   * Subscribes for one delivery. Removed before it is called, so it runs once
   * even if it throws.
   */
  once<K extends keyof E>(event: K, handler: EventHandler<E[K]>): () => void {
    return this.add(event, handler, true);
  }

  /**
   * Unsubscribes. Silent when the handler was not subscribed, which is the
   * useful behaviour for teardown.
   */
  off<K extends keyof E>(event: K, handler: EventHandler<E[K]>): void {
    this.registry[event]?.delete(handler);
  }

  /**
   * How many handlers would run. Mostly for tests, where it is the only way to
   * see a removal happened.
   */
  listenerCount(event: keyof E): number {
    return this.registry[event]?.size ?? 0;
  }

  /**
   * Announces an event to everyone subscribed to it.
   *
   * Returns nothing, so the emitting code is not coupled to what its
   * subscribers do. That is the usual reason to reach for an emitter, and the
   * cost is that an asynchronous handler's work is not waited for.
   */
  emit<K extends keyof E>(event: K, ...payload: E[K]): void {
    const registered = this.registry[event];
    if (registered === undefined) return;

    // Snapshotted before anything is called, so a handler that subscribes
    // during dispatch is not called by the dispatch that created it — which
    // would otherwise be a loop that feeds itself.
    const snapshot = [...registered];

    // Single-delivery registrations are dropped up front rather than after
    // being called, so `once` means at most once even if the handler throws.
    for (const [handler, once] of snapshot)
      if (once) registered.delete(handler);

    for (const [handler, once] of snapshot) {
      // A handler removed during this dispatch does not run. The snapshot alone
      // would deliver to it, which is what the copied-array implementations do;
      // a subscriber that has torn itself down has said it wants no more
      // events, and an emit already under way is no exception. The entries
      // removed just above are exempt, since they are meant to be called
      // exactly here.
      if (!once && !registered.has(handler)) continue;

      try {
        handler(...payload);
      } catch (error) {
        this.onError(error, event);
      }
    }
  }

  private add<K extends keyof E>(
    event: K,
    handler: EventHandler<E[K]>,
    once: boolean,
  ): () => void {
    const handlers =
      this.registry[event] ?? new Map<EventHandler<E[K]>, boolean>();
    handlers.set(handler, once);
    this.registry[event] = handlers;

    return () => {
      handlers.delete(handler);
    };
  }
}

/**
 * The emitter for OrderEvents.
 *
 * A subclass rather than a type alias, so that it can be constructed by name.
 * This is the only place the event map is named, and the only type a caller
 * needs.
 */
export class OrderEmitter extends TypedEmitter<OrderEvents> {}
```

## order-emitter-example.ts (example)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern typed-emitter
 * @options f4f2afcf27974e2a
 */

/**
 * Subscribing, emitting, and the things that will not compile.
 *
 * The refusals at the end are assertions rather than illustrations:
 * `@ts-expect-error` is satisfied by an error and violated by silence, so each
 * states that the line below it must not compile. They are emitted whether or
 * not tests were asked for, because they are the entire reason to reach for a
 * typed emitter over an untyped one and no suite that runs can check any of
 * them.
 */

import { OrderEmitter } from "./order-emitter.js";
import type { OrderEventName } from "./order-emitter.js";

/**
 * Where a subscriber's failure is reported.
 *
 * Isolation is only defensible if this exists. A handler that throws is not the
 * emitter's fault and must not become the emitting code's problem, but it is
 * still a fault, and somewhere has to hear about it.
 */
function report(error: unknown, event: OrderEventName): void {
  console.error(`handler for ${event} failed`, error);
}

/**
 * Subscribing.
 *
 * The handler's parameters are named and typed from the event map, with nothing
 * annotated here: `id` is a `string` and `amount` is a `number` because the map
 * says so, and a handler that expected otherwise would not compile.
 */
export const orders = new OrderEmitter({ onError: report });

export const stopWatchingPayments = orders.on("paid", (id, amount) => {
  console.log(`${id} paid ${String(amount)}`);
});

// A handler is free to ignore what it does not need, including all of it.
export const stopWatchingOpens = orders.on("opened", () => {
  console.log("opened");
});

/**
 * Emitting.
 *
 * `emit` returns nothing, so the emitting code neither waits for its
 * subscribers nor learns what they did.
 */
export function record(id: string, amount: number): void {
  orders.emit("paid", id, amount);

  // A zero-argument event takes no arguments at all.
  orders.emit("opened");
}

/**
 * Unsubscribing.
 *
 * Two ways, for two situations. The function returned by `on` cannot be called
 * with the wrong event or the wrong handler, because it closes over both, and
 * is what to use where the subscription and its teardown are near each other.
 * `off` is for where they are not.
 */
export function stopEverything(
  handler: (id: string, reason: string) => void,
): void {
  stopWatchingPayments();
  stopWatchingOpens();
  orders.off("cancelled", handler);
}

/**
 * The refusals, asserted.
 *
 * Each directive sits alone on its line with the reason above it, because a
 * directive governs only the line it begins on and a long comment gets
 * re-wrapped by the formatter.
 *
 * Where the mistake is one argument of a call, the directive sits inside the
 * argument list, above that argument. Above the whole call it would hold only
 * until the call grew wide enough to wrap — which a long enough type name is
 * sufficient to cause — and then the error is reported against the argument's
 * own line while the directive governs the receiver's, so the assertion inverts
 * into two errors: the escaped mistake, and a directive with nothing to
 * suppress. A comment among arguments also keeps the formatter from collapsing
 * them, so the shape holds for a short name too.
 */

export function refusesAnUnknownEvent(): void {
  // The typo that an untyped emitter accepts in silence, subscribing to or
  // announcing something no one will ever hear. Here it is a compile error at
  // the line that has it.
  orders.emit(
    // @ts-expect-error
    "payed",
    "A-1",
    100,
  );
}

export function refusesAMistypedPayload(): void {
  // The amount is a number, and a string that looks like one is not it.
  orders.emit(
    "paid",
    "A-1",
    // @ts-expect-error
    "100",
  );
}

export function refusesAnIncompletePayload(): void {
  // Every element the tuple declares is required. An emitter that let this
  // through would call its handlers with `undefined` where they were promised a
  // number.
  //
  // @ts-expect-error
  orders.emit("paid", "A-1");
}

export function refusesAMismatchedHandler(): void {
  // The first element of the payload is a string. A handler declaring it
  // otherwise is refused here rather than at the moment the event is announced.
  orders.on(
    "paid",
    // @ts-expect-error
    (id: number) => {
      console.log(id);
    },
  );
}

export function refusesASurplusParameter(): void {
  // Fewer parameters than the payload is fine; more is not, since there would
  // be nothing to pass.
  orders.on(
    "cancelled",
    // @ts-expect-error
    (id: string, reason: string, extra: string) => {
      console.log(id, reason, extra);
    },
  );
}

export function refusesAMissingErrorSink(): void {
  // Isolation without a sink is silence, so the sink is required rather than
  // defaulted.
  //
  // @ts-expect-error
  new OrderEmitter();
}
```

## order-emitter.test-d.ts (test)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern typed-emitter
 * @options f4f2afcf27974e2a
 */

/**
 * What the compiler is asked to prove.
 *
 * Nothing here runs. The suffix keeps the file out of every runner while
 * leaving it in front of the compiler, which is the only thing that can check
 * these claims — an emitter whose payload types had quietly widened to
 * `unknown` would deliver exactly the same values at run time.
 *
 * No claim below concerns nullability. Bundles are verified at every
 * strictness, and with `strictNullChecks` off `undefined` is assignable to
 * everything, so such an assertion would mean one thing for one caller and the
 * opposite for another.
 */

import { OrderEmitter } from "./order-emitter.js";
import type {
  EventHandler,
  OrderEventName,
  OrderEvents,
} from "./order-emitter.js";

/**
 * Forces its argument to be `true`, and fails to compile when it is not.
 *
 * Each assertion below is written as a named alias rather than a bare one, so
 * that it reads as a stated claim about the code and cannot be mistaken for a
 * leftover.
 */
export type Expect<T extends true> = T;

/**
 * Whether two types are identical, rather than merely assignable in both
 * directions.
 *
 * The two-function form looks like a trick because it is one: it compares the
 * types in a position the compiler checks by identity instead of by
 * assignability. The obvious alternative — asking whether each extends the
 * other — answers a different question, and answers it wrongly in two common
 * cases. It reports `true` for `any` against anything at all, and it
 * distributes over unions, so a union compared against one of its own members
 * can come back true.
 */
export type Equal<X, Y> =
  (<T>() => T extends X ? 1 : 2) extends <T>() => T extends Y ? 1 : 2
    ? true
    : false;

/**
 * Whether `X` is assignable to `Y`.
 *
 * Both sides are wrapped in a tuple to stop the union distribution a bare
 * conditional performs. Undistributed is the question that was meant: whether
 * the whole of `X` is acceptable as a `Y`, rather than whether each member of
 * it is on its own.
 */
export type Extends<X, Y> = [X] extends [Y] ? true : false;

/**
 * Whether `X` is rejected where a `Y` is wanted.
 *
 * The type-level counterpart to `@ts-expect-error`, and preferable wherever the
 * claim is about a relationship rather than about a particular line: a
 * directive suppresses whichever error occurs, so it can be satisfied by an
 * unrelated mistake on the same line, where this cannot.
 */
export type NotAssignable<X, Y> = [X] extends [Y] ? false : true;

/**
 * The payload types reach the handler's parameters.
 *
 * The claim the whole pattern rests on, stated where it can be checked: the
 * tuple in the event map is exactly what a handler for that event receives.
 */
export type PaidPayload = Expect<
  Equal<OrderEvents["paid"], [id: string, amount: number]>
>;
export type OpenedPayloadIsEmpty = Expect<Equal<OrderEvents["opened"], []>>;

/**
 * The event names are closed.
 *
 * `NotAssignable` rather than a directive, because this states something about
 * the type itself rather than about one line that uses it: no string outside
 * the map is a name, so nothing can subscribe to an event that does not exist.
 */
export type NamesAreClosed = Expect<
  Equal<OrderEventName, "opened" | "paid" | "cancelled">
>;
export type ArbitraryStringIsNotAName = Expect<
  NotAssignable<"payed", OrderEventName>
>;

/**
 * A handler may take fewer parameters than the event carries, and not more.
 *
 * Both directions, because the permissive half is often mistaken for a defect
 * and the restrictive half is what actually protects the handler: there would
 * be nothing to pass a fourth parameter.
 */
export type FewerParametersAccepted = Expect<
  Extends<() => void, EventHandler<OrderEvents["paid"]>>
>;
export type SurplusParametersRefused = Expect<
  NotAssignable<
    (id: string, amount: number, extra: string) => void,
    EventHandler<OrderEvents["paid"]>
  >
>;

/**
 * Unsubscribing is returned, not described.
 *
 * A small claim with a practical point: the value `on` hands back is callable
 * with no arguments, so a caller cannot get the event or the handler wrong when
 * tearing the subscription down.
 */
declare const orders: OrderEmitter;
export type SubscribingReturnsATeardown = Expect<
  Equal<ReturnType<OrderEmitter["on"]>, () => void>
>;

/**
 * Emitting returns nothing, and a handler's return value is discarded.
 *
 * Stated because it is the one hole in this rendering — an `async` handler is
 * accepted here, and `emit` will not wait for it, so a rejection inside it goes
 * unobserved. Asynchronous dispatch is the rendering that closes it.
 */
export type EmitReturns = Expect<Equal<ReturnType<OrderEmitter["emit"]>, void>>;
export type AsyncHandlerAccepted = Expect<
  Extends<() => Promise<void>, EventHandler<OrderEvents["opened"]>>
>;
void orders;
```

## order-emitter.test.ts (test)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern typed-emitter
 * @options f4f2afcf27974e2a
 */

/**
 * What is left for a suite that runs.
 *
 * Not the payload types, which are settled before this file executes and
 * asserted in `order-emitter.test-d.ts`. What remains is the behaviour no type
 * can describe: who is called, in what order, exactly once, and what happens to
 * the rest when one of them fails.
 */

import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";

import { OrderEmitter } from "./order-emitter.js";

/**
 * A recorder for what handlers saw.
 *
 * `note` returns `void`, which is why every handler below can be a concise
 * arrow: pushing to the array directly would return its new length, and under
 * asynchronous dispatch the handler type does not accept a returned value. See
 * the note on that type.
 */
function recorder(): {
  readonly seen: string[];
  readonly note: (line: string) => void;
} {
  const lines: string[] = [];

  return {
    seen: lines,
    note: (line) => {
      lines.push(line);
    },
  };
}

/**
 * An emitter for the cases that are not about failure.
 *
 * The sink rethrows rather than ignoring, because a handler failing in a test
 * about delivery order is a fact that test needs to hear. Swallowing it would
 * turn a broken handler into a mysteriously short list.
 */
function emitter(): OrderEmitter {
  return new OrderEmitter({
    onError: (error) => {
      throw error;
    },
  });
}

/**
 * A sink that records rather than reports, so a test can assert what reached
 * it.
 */
function collector(): {
  readonly failures: unknown[];
  readonly onError: (error: unknown) => void;
} {
  const failures: unknown[] = [];

  return { failures, onError: (error) => failures.push(error) };
}

describe("subscribing and emitting", () => {
  it("delivers the payload to every subscriber", () => {
    const orders = emitter();
    const { seen, note } = recorder();

    orders.on("paid", (id, amount) => note(`a:${id}:${String(amount)}`));
    orders.on("paid", (id) => note(`b:${id}`));
    orders.emit("paid", "A-1", 100);

    expect(seen).toEqual(["a:A-1:100", "b:A-1"]);
  });

  it("delivers in registration order", () => {
    const orders = emitter();
    const { seen, note } = recorder();

    for (const label of ["first", "second", "third"]) {
      orders.on("opened", () => note(label));
    }
    orders.emit("opened");

    expect(seen).toEqual(["first", "second", "third"]);
  });

  it("does nothing for an event with no subscribers", () => {
    const orders = emitter();

    orders.emit("opened");

    expect(orders.listenerCount("opened")).toBe(0);
  });

  it("registers a handler once, however many times it is added", () => {
    const orders = emitter();
    const { seen, note } = recorder();
    const handler = (): void => note("x");

    orders.on("opened", handler);
    orders.on("opened", handler);
    orders.emit("opened");

    expect(seen).toEqual(["x"]);
    expect(orders.listenerCount("opened")).toBe(1);
  });
});

describe("unsubscribing", () => {
  it("stops delivery through the returned teardown", () => {
    const orders = emitter();
    const { seen, note } = recorder();
    const stop = orders.on("opened", () => note("x"));

    stop();
    orders.emit("opened");

    expect(seen).toEqual([]);
    expect(orders.listenerCount("opened")).toBe(0);
  });

  it("stops delivery through off", () => {
    const orders = emitter();
    const { seen, note } = recorder();
    const handler = (): void => note("x");

    orders.on("opened", handler);
    orders.off("opened", handler);
    orders.emit("opened");

    expect(seen).toEqual([]);
  });

  it("is silent about a handler that was never subscribed", () => {
    // Silence rather than a throw, because teardown often runs on a path that
    // is not sure whether the subscription happened, and an emitter that
    // punished that would make every caller check first.
    const orders = emitter();

    orders.off("opened", () => undefined);

    expect(orders.listenerCount("opened")).toBe(0);
  });
});

describe("once", () => {
  it("delivers exactly one time", () => {
    const orders = emitter();
    const { seen, note } = recorder();

    orders.once("paid", (id) => note(id));
    orders.on("paid", (id) => note(`always:${id}`));
    orders.emit("paid", "A-1", 100);
    orders.emit("paid", "A-2", 200);

    expect(seen).toEqual(["A-1", "always:A-1", "always:A-2"]);
  });

  it("can be cancelled before it ever fires", () => {
    const orders = emitter();
    const { seen, note } = recorder();
    const stop = orders.once("opened", () => note("x"));

    stop();
    orders.emit("opened");

    expect(seen).toEqual([]);
  });
});

describe("a registry changed while it is being read", () => {
  it("does not deliver to a handler subscribed during the dispatch", () => {
    // The snapshot, asserted. Without it this dispatch would call the handler
    // it just created, and a handler that subscribes unconditionally would
    // never stop.
    const orders = emitter();
    const { seen, note } = recorder();

    orders.on("opened", () => {
      note("first");
      orders.on("opened", () => note("added"));
    });
    orders.on("opened", () => note("second"));
    orders.emit("opened");

    expect(seen).toEqual(["first", "second"]);

    // It is subscribed, though — the next dispatch reaches it.
    orders.emit("opened");

    expect(seen).toEqual(["first", "second", "first", "second", "added"]);
  });

  it("does not deliver to a handler unsubscribed during the dispatch", () => {
    // The membership check, asserted. The snapshot alone would deliver here,
    // which is what the copied-array implementations do and is wrong: this
    // handler has said it wants no more events.
    const orders = emitter();
    const { seen, note } = recorder();
    const doomed = (): void => note("doomed");

    orders.on("opened", () => {
      note("first");
      orders.off("opened", doomed);
    });
    orders.on("opened", doomed);
    orders.emit("opened");

    expect(seen).toEqual(["first"]);
  });
});

describe("a failing subscriber", () => {
  it("does not stop the others, and is reported", () => {
    const sink = collector();
    const orders = new OrderEmitter({ onError: sink.onError });
    const { seen, note } = recorder();

    orders.on("opened", () => note("before"));
    orders.on("opened", () => {
      throw new Error("boom");
    });
    orders.on("opened", () => note("after"));
    orders.emit("opened");

    // The subscriber after the failure is the one that matters: it had nothing
    // to do with the fault and would have silently lost the event.
    expect(seen).toEqual(["before", "after"]);
    expect(sink.failures).toHaveLength(1);
  });

  it("does not become the emitting code's problem", () => {
    const sink = collector();
    const orders = new OrderEmitter({ onError: sink.onError });

    orders.on("opened", () => {
      throw new Error("boom");
    });

    // Isolation means this returns normally. The failure is in the sink, not
    // here.
    orders.emit("opened");

    expect(sink.failures).toHaveLength(1);
  });

  it("is still removed when it was registered for one delivery", () => {
    const sink = collector();
    const orders = new OrderEmitter({ onError: sink.onError });

    orders.once("opened", () => {
      throw new Error("boom");
    });
    orders.emit("opened");

    // Removed before being called, so a throwing handler does not get a second
    // chance.
    expect(orders.listenerCount("opened")).toBe(0);
    expect(sink.failures).toHaveLength(1);
  });
});
```
